title: Antonelli reveals 'incredible' messages after becoming champion
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli admits that "the support has been incredible" since he became Formula 1's youngest World Champion, and has revealed his favourite messages ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Antonelli secured the 2026 title in his sophomore season last weekend after finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming World Champion at the age of just 20.

The Mercedes driver beat the record for the youngest champion previously held by Sebastian Vettel, and revealed on Thursday's media day in Brazil that a video from the four-time World Champion had been a personal favourite amongst many.

"It’s been an amazing two days, but I still haven’t had enough time to realise and digest what has just happened. Definitely, I’m very happy. It still feels surreal," said Antonelli.

"I’ve received so many nice messages, so much support, and I’ve had a lot of videos from my hometown celebrating. The support has been incredible. It’s really hard to pick one single moment or one single action that impressed me the most because they were all super nice.

"But I think the message from Seb was very nice. It was very deep, with a lot of meaning behind it and a lot of advice for the future. So that was very nice.

"But I also got a lot from other drivers, from Max, Lewis, Charles. Everyone was super nice. Lando was super nice to me as well. So I’m very happy and grateful to see so much respect and support.

"I’ve also had the chance to recharge and enjoy a couple of days doing some really nice activities, especially spending time with the Senna family. That was truly incredible and something that I will remember forever.

"So yes, it’s been very demanding in some ways, but I’ve had the time and the chance to relax and recharge. It was also very nice to see so much excitement and support around me."

Mercedes can still claim the teams' title this weekend in Brazil and Antonelli admits beyond that, he is looking to just enjoy the remaining races while fighting for the wins.

"The goal coming here is to win. It’s a track that I love, and the fans are amazing here. So I’m really looking forward to it," said Antonelli.

"The goal is to have a great weekend, but also to enjoy the rest of the season. Obviously, we’ve still got races to go, races where we want to do well. So I’m looking forward to it. It’s definitely a really cool place to start everything again after clinching the title and to get a win."

title: Why Russell had ‘to get out’ after Antonelli’s title win
excerpt:
George Russell has confessed that he needed “to just get out” after a frustrating race in Mexico City, combined with seeing team mate Kimi Antonelli secure the Drivers’ Championship, left him to rue his “rubbish season”.

With a P3 finish, the Italian secured the title for good as it’s now mathematically impossible for any other driver to surpass his 380 points in the remaining rounds, making him the youngest champion in F1 history.

Although Antonelli’s triumph was highly likely heading into the Mexico City Grand Prix, Russell at least had a chance of victory after he missed out on pole position by just 0.009s to Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

However, his hopes of challenging for the lead disappeared when a deployment issue impacted his start, which caused him to drop down the order before making contact with Isack Hadjar. Adding to his woes, he received a 10-second time penalty for the incident and ultimately wound up sixth.

“I was extremely disappointed Sunday night, more from the fact of missing out on a great result from something again outside of my control, and that was just a really tough pill to swallow,” Russell explained in Sao Paulo.

“This season it’s been ‘tough moment, pick yourself back up, tough moment, pick yourself back up’. And I think, as an individual, I’ve continued to have that resilience of being able to always pick myself back up, and it kind of just got to the point in me where I was like, ‘I need to just get out of here’, because it’s just been relentless what’s happened this year.

“It’s been tough. I’m here, four days later, ready to go again. And I think for any individual, or sportsperson, or businessperson, you never have every year of your life that goes the way you want.

“We all have problems we deal with. We have good days, bad days, good years, bad years. I think it’s important to not let that define you – you’ve just got to come back stronger, and that’s what we’re here to do.”

The overwhelming day also saw Russell skip his post-race media duties and take time away from the track, with the numerous reliability problems he’s endured this season still fresh on his mind.

From a power unit failure whilst leading the Canadian Grand Prix to repeated straight line speed deployment troubles, the Briton’s title ambitions were partly limited by the performance of his W17.

He admitted: “I don’t think I’ve ever had this many setbacks in my career. I went through – after the race with my engineer – the season race by race, and we realised we had six races this season with no issues, and 14 races where we’ve had an issue of some sort.

“To give perspective, in the years gone by, we would maybe have two races where there were issues, or I think in 2023 we had four races where we had issues. This season we’ve had 14 races.

“I’ve always sort of picked myself back up. As much as I love talking to [the media] after the race, I didn’t really fancy it on this occasion, so I was like, ‘I’m going to just get out of here and go for a nice dinner and think about something other than the rubbish season we’ve had’.”

title: Hamilton wants Ferrari talks in Brazil after Mexico battle
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton admits that face-to-face talks between himself and Ferrari team mate Charles Leclerc need to take place at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix this weekend after their on-track battle in Mexico.

Hamilton started on pole and finished second last weekend at the Mexico City Grand Prix, but believed a potential 1-2 was lost after going side-by-side with Leclerc on the opening lap.

Leclerc was handed a penalty for cutting the track, while Hamilton dropped behind Max Verstappen and was never able to recover the position.

Speaking on Thursday ahead of the Sao Paulo weekend, Hamilton said talks between himself and Leclerc were yet to take place as the Monegasque driver was back home due to the birth of his first child, while Team Principal Fred Vasseur had also been back in Europe at the factory.

"The energy in the team is really great. I think they've been doing an amazing job. We've really done a great job in these last few races, scored more points than anybody," said Hamilton.

"I think we really levelled up, I would say particularly over the last four races with some changes we've implemented and our execution has been so much better, which is what we've been working towards.

"I'm so happy to see that. Of course, we should have easily had a 1-2 last race and so we've got to work to make sure that [it] never happens again. Ultimately, I 100% know my responsibility for the team, that's never wavered and never will."

While unhappy about the situation in Mexico, Hamilton admitted that having an intra-team battle this season, which has brought up issues, was better to have in 2026 with the championships already lost.

The seven-time World Champion also believes that setting a foundation and rules of engagement will be imperative if Ferrari are to challenge for the title in 2027.

"I don't think everything is going to get squashed and sorted out in one meeting but it is important," added Hamilton.

"What we build now will put us in the right position for next year. In some ways, I'm glad we had that experience.

"Of course, I'd rather we won and had a 1-2, but from that you can learn and we can only really get stronger."

title: A 'big surprise to be second' in the standings – Verstappen
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has revealed that it’s “a big surprise” to be as high up as second in the drivers’ standings after Red Bull suffered a challenging start to the 2026 season, with the Dutchman praising the team for never giving up.

It took five rounds before the four-time World Champion finished on the podium, and 16 events until he returned to winning ways, but Verstappen’s consistency since the summer break has seen him improve to P2 with a slim advantage over Lewis Hamilton.

Red Bull fully leaned into the development battle and introduced effective upgrades in order to facilitate their progress, which Verstappen admitted he wouldn’t have been able to foresee earlier in the year.

“It's a big surprise to be second, to be honest, in the championship, but we take it,” the Dutchman said ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix. “I think we had a lot of difficulties as a team in the beginning. You know, the car was not where we wanted it to be.

“Probably also, we still had to learn quite a bit from the power unit, and I think we really learned a lot throughout the season. The car has naturally been a lot more competitive, of course, lately.

“From my side, it’s just you never really give up, or you just never really settle for P6 or P7. Even when I was in that position or fighting the midfield, I was still trying to do the best that I could get out of the situation – sometimes that is a P6, when the car is not able to perform better.

“Once the car is in a better window, then you can fight further up front and eventually win races. Of course when you win, you take points out of everyone else, so that's been the scene for the last races.

“I’m happy with that, but it also shows that the team never gave up and they were really pushing to find these improvements and understand the difficulties. I'm just happy that within a season, we had such a big turnaround.”

Although Red Bull have made significant gains over the second half of the season, Verstappen has still faced issues with his radio communication and downshifts over recent race weekends.

Asked how he has worked with the team to adapt, he explained: “The radio was, I think, a lot better in Mexico. We were also trying some things and it's just a few tiny settings probably to still get right. But actually the team was hearing me very well – maybe everyone else [was] not, but that's actually fantastic to be honest, so we should actually try and keep it that way.

“With shifts or whatever that you hear me complain about, it’s just because I'm never satisfied because I think certain things can be better and I always try to fine tune or find improvements.

“If you hear it as complaining, it's more for me to make sure that the team is always looking into details to try and find more lap time because I know there is more lap time in it."

title: 'I don’t know what else they want me to do’– Lawson on his future
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has admitted that he doesn’t “know what else they want me to do” as his future at Racing Bulls remains uncertain, with the New Zealander focused on “trying to show my best every weekend”.

Team Principal Alan Permane previously explained that they have three contenders for two seats in 2027 – namely Lawson, his current team mate Arvid Lindblad, and Red Bull Junior Nikola Tsolov.

While the latter completed his first FP1 outing at the Mexico City Grand Prix and finished P12, 0.126s adrift of Lindblad, Lawson believes that his own performances have amounted to a strong campaign for Racing Bulls.

Asked ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix whether his recent results – which include a trio of P7 finishes in Bahrain, Singapore and Mexico – should secure his seat, he replied: “I don’t know. I mean, every weekend I’ve been trying to obviously do my best.

“But we’ve had a really strong year and we’re in a good position. We’re fighting Alpine. We’re pulling away from Alpine every weekend, and with a few races left, we’re trying to stay on top of them.

“I don’t know what else they want me to do, but yeah, it’s just one of those things at the moment.”

The majority of teams have already announced their 2027 driver line-ups, so if Lawson were to be replaced at Racing Bulls, he would likely need to consider moving into a reserve role in order to remain in F1.

Probed further on whether he has a back-up plan, he said: “I mean, it’s tough, isn’t it? It’s the end of the season.

“When something like this is pushed all the way to the end, you’re left with not really any options, so it’s not the easiest situation. Obviously, I want to be racing in F1, and I’m trying to show my best every weekend. I feel like we’ve had a good year.”

Lawson has netted 83 points so far and sits ninth in the standings as the ‘best of the rest’ driver, with an advantage of 42 points over his nearest competitor – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly.

His consistent top-10 finishes have also helped Racing Bulls grab a commanding hold on P5 in the Constructors’ Championship, which would represent their best-ever result as a team, even going all the way back to their roots as Minardi.

It’s therefore of little surprise that Lawson considers this season to be “a lot stronger” than his other stints in F1, especially after he charged from the pit lane to P7 last time out in Mexico City.

“This year, I haven’t really thought about [the uncertainty] so much, but also the racing has been a lot stronger this year,” he explained. “I think Mexico was more of a specific situation that obviously happened on Friday and made the whole weekend a bit tougher, but in terms of performance, I was in the same place I’ve been all year.

“I feel like the speed’s been good, and in Mexico it was very, very good. Obviously, we qualified very, very well. I just had the penalty and had to start from the pit lane. But I think outside of that, we were quick all weekend.

“The race pace was good. We were able to come through. I don’t see why we shouldn’t be quick here. I feel like it’s a track that I enjoy driving, and the car should work well. I think the bigger question is the weather over the weekend.”

title: Bottas offers update on Cadillac F1 future
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas admits that his Cadillac Formula 1 future "should be okay" amid speculation that the Finn will not be retained by the American team next season.

Bottas returned to F1 after a season on the sidelines with Mercedes as part of Cadillac's venture into the sport, with the 10-time Grand Prix winner partnering Sergio Perez to form one of the championship's most experienced line-ups.

But while Perez's future was confirmed ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix last weekend, Bottas has still yet to be confirmed despite initially signing a multi-year contract. That's because the American squad are yet to commit to triggering an option in his contract that would keep him in the seat for 2027.

Ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix this weekend, Bottas was asked about his future and whether he will be racing on the grid next season.

"In my head, it should be okay," he said. "You know, that’s what I signed up for, for the long term. And, I haven’t heard anything other than that, so in my head, it should be all good."

Speculation has grown that his spot in the team could be taken by reserve driver and IndyCar winner, Colton Herta. While the American has struggled to make an impact in F2, and sits 19th in the standings, he has impressed the team when behind the wheel of a Cadillac during his Free Practice 1 sessions this year.

So far the American has made five FP1 appearances for Cadillac in a bid to gain enough Super Licence points to earn an F1 spot if one becomes available, with a sixth FP1 to come in Sao Paulo as he takes the place of Sergio Perez.

"It kind of makes sense for him because I understood that if he misses the Super Licence this year, then it’s going to be almost impossible to get it," said Bottas.

"And as long as he gets it now, it’s going to be valid for a few years. So I’m pretty sure the team wants to have that just in case, not necessarily for next year. So that’s at least what I hope.

"But from my side, nothing has changed. The team has told me they don’t want to change anything. So that’s where we are."

Bottas suffered a spectacular exit from the Grand Prix last weekend after the front-left suspension on his car failed, sending him into the barrier at Turn 1.

Having recovered from a bruised knee, Bottas claimed he still had full confidence in the team despite a spate of mechanical and reliability issues which means he has retired from nine Grands Prix so far this season.

"It’s never nice when that kind of thing happens on track," he said. "It shouldn’t happen, but it happened.

"And the best thing we can do is to understand, find the cause, why it exactly happened and how to make sure that it never happens again.

"And I believe that is what we’ve done, so that’s why I will trust the car again when I get out there."

title: Camara explains approach as he prepares for F1 debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara states he will "focus on things that I can control" as the Brazilian prepares to make his Formula 1 debut with Haas at his home event in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Camara will compete in his first F1 event this weekend, with Haas confirming Esteban Ocon will no longer compete for them for the remainder of the season after the Frenchman was replaced during the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Ryo Hirakawa stepped into the role as Haas' reserve driver last weekend, eventually being classified 10th on his F1 debut, but the Japanese driver is racing for Toyota in the World Endurance Championship this weekend.

This has opened the door for Camara to step up from F2 earlier than expected with the Brazilian having already been confirmed with Haas for the 2027 season.

Speaking during Thursday's media day in Sao Paulo, Camara admitted he was trying not to put pressure on himself, having never driven either Haas' 2026 car or at the Interlagos circuit before, and with his debut coming at his home event.

"I think for myself, whatever people are speaking about or whatever is happening outside has never really been a problem," he said.

"So I think it should be alright. It should not be a problem. And like I said, I always try to just focus on my side, focus on things that I can control, and whatever is happening outside is not really in my control."

Despite being thrust into the seat, Camara was able to conduct simulator work ahead of the weekend as a Ferrari junior driver, while three, one-hour practice sessions will help him get up to speed on track.

"I still did some simulator work with Ferrari because I was supposed to have FP1 [as a young driver later in the year], so it was good to have some laps on the simulator," he said.

"Some days before coming to Brazil, but it was in the other [older] car. I’ve never driven here, but with these simulator sessions, I think it should be alright. We have three sessions, and then definitely you can build from these sessions."

Camara's move up to F1 comes as he sits at the top of the F2 standings in just his rookie campaign with two rounds remaining in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Haas have yet to confirm if Camara will compete for the American team in those remaining outings, with the 21-year-old stating "that is something that is still to come and still in the future", with his focus entirely on this weekend.

title: Hamilton's incredible F1 records ahead of his 400th GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is set to reach another Formula 1 milestone at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix as he prepares for his 400th Grand Prix appearance. Ahead of the occasion, F1.com looks at some of the remarkable records held by the seven-time World Champion.

The Briton has rewritten the F1 history books on numerous occasions since making his debut with McLaren at the 2007 Australian Grand Prix. Now in his 20th season, the Ferrari driver is preparing to add another marker to a career that has already featured 106 victories, 105 pole positions and seven World Championships.

Ahead of his weekend in Brazil, F1.com takes a look at some of the extraordinary records held by Lewis Hamilton…

Most World Championships (joint) – 7

When Hamilton claimed his maiden World Championship in dramatic fashion at the 2008 Brazilian Grand Prix, few could have predicted just how many more titles would follow.

After narrowly missing out on the crown during his rookie campaign in 2007, the Briton secured his first title a year later before adding another six during his hugely successful spell with Mercedes.

His seventh championship, sealed at the 2020 Turkish Grand Prix, saw Hamilton draw level with Michael Schumacher's long-standing record, making the pair the most successful drivers in F1 history in terms of titles won.

Most Grand Prix victories – 106

Hamilton first tasted victory at the 2007 Canadian Grand Prix, just six races into his Formula 1 career. Little did he know that it would be the first of more than 100 wins.

At the 2020 Portuguese Grand Prix, the Mercedes driver claimed his 92nd victory to surpass Schumacher's previous record, before becoming the first driver in F1 history to reach a century of wins at the 2021 Russian Grand Prix.

And the victories have continued into 2026, with Hamilton taking his maiden triumph for Ferrari at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix to bring his record-breaking tally to 106.

Most pole positions – 105

Hamilton's impressive one-lap pace has been evident since his rookie season, when he claimed his first pole position at the 2007 Canadian Grand Prix. A decade later, he surpassed Schumacher's record of 68 poles at the 2017 Italian Grand Prix, becoming the most successful qualifier in F1 history.

Having become the first driver to reach 100 pole positions in Spain in 2021, Hamilton extended his record even further at the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix, edging out George Russell by just 0.009s to claim his 105th pole and his first for the Scuderia.

Most podium finishes – 209

Hamilton wasted little time making an impression in Formula 1, finishing third on his debut at the 2007 Australian Grand Prix before going on to stand on the podium at each of his first nine races. That remarkable start was just a sign of things to come, with the Briton surpassing Schumacher's record of 155 podium finishes at the 2020 Spanish Grand Prix.

More than six years later, Hamilton continues to add to his tally, with his second-place finish at the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix marking his 209th podium appearance, more than any other driver in F1 history.

Most wins with a single constructor – 84

Hamilton's decision to leave McLaren for Mercedes ahead of the 2013 season would prove to be one of the most significant moves of his career.

Having secured his maiden victory for the Silver Arrows at the 2013 Hungarian Grand Prix, Hamilton went on to enjoy a period of extraordinary success with the team, claiming six World Championships and helping Mercedes establish themselves as a dominant force in the sport.

By the time their partnership came to an end in 2024, Hamilton had secured an incredible 84 Grand Prix victories with Mercedes, the most achieved by any driver with a single constructor.

The inside story of Lewis Hamilton's first F1 test

Most victories at a single circuit – 9

There is something about Silverstone that brings out the best in Hamilton, with the British driver having enjoyed more success at his home circuit than any other racer has managed at a single venue. His first victory there came in treacherous conditions at the 2008 British Grand Prix, when he crossed the line more than a minute clear of his nearest rival.

Eight further victories followed, including an emotional triumph in 2024 that ended a winless run of more than two years and took his Silverstone tally to a record nine wins, surpassing Schumacher's eight wins at Magny-Cours.

Longest winning career – 19 years and four days

Almost two decades separated Hamilton's first Grand Prix victory in Canada in 2007 and his landmark first win for Ferrari at the 2026 Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix. That triumph did more than extend his record-breaking tally of victories to 106. It also saw Hamilton claim another piece of F1 history, setting a new benchmark for the longest span between a driver's first and most recent Grand Prix wins.

At 19 years and four days, the Briton surpassed the previous record held by Kimi Raikkonen, whose first victory at the 2003 Malaysian Grand Prix and final win at the 2018 United States Grand Prix were separated by 15 years, six months and 28 days.

Longest pole position career – 19 years, four months and 22 days

And Hamilton's longevity is not just reflected in his race victories, with the seven-time World Champion also holding the record for the longest span between a driver's first and most recent pole positions.

Having first topped Qualifying at the 2007 Canadian Grand Prix, Hamilton added another pole to his tally more than 19 years later at the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix.

The achievement extended the record to an extraordinary 19 years, four months and 22 days, putting him ahead of Kimi Raikkonen, whose first pole at the 2003 European Grand Prix and final pole at the 2018 Italian Grand Prix were separated by 15 years, two months and four days.

Most consecutive points finishes – 48

While Hamilton's victories and pole positions often steal the headlines, his remarkable consistency has also earned him a place in the history books. Starting at the 2018 British Grand Prix, the Mercedes driver embarked on an incredible run of 48 consecutive points finishes, extending all the way to the 2020 Bahrain Grand Prix.

Most consecutive seasons with a podium finish – 18

Hamilton's ability to consistently challenge at the front of the field is reflected in another remarkable record, having secured at least one Grand Prix podium in 18 consecutive Formula 1 seasons. The streak, which stretched from his rookie campaign in 2007 to his final season with Mercedes in 2024, set a new F1 benchmark and underlined the Briton's ability to compete at the front across multiple generations of cars and regulations.

Although the streak came to an end during his maiden season with Ferrari in 2025, Hamilton returned to the podium in 2026, proving that he still has plenty more to give as he approaches his 400th Grand Prix.

The sequence was interrupted when Hamilton was forced to miss the subsequent Sakhir Grand Prix after testing positive for COVID-19, but his tally remains the benchmark for consecutive points-scoring finishes in Formula 1.

title: Remembering Williams' first World Champion Alan Jones
excerpt:
Aussie Battler may be one of those hackneyed nicknames for all Australian sportsmen but it was a title that fitted Alan Jones – who died on Thursday, three days after his 80th birthday – to a tee.

A genuine tough guy from Melbourne, he didn’t need molly-coddling by anyone but rose through the motorsport ranks to become World Champion with Williams in 1980 through a combination of bloody-mindedness and sheer grit.

His father Stan was one of those larger-than-life personalities. He was a farmer, but also ran a successful motor business selling up to 300 Holdens a month, and owned a series of dramatic Maybach-engined cars which he raced with gusto. His son was often there in the huge entourage he would take with him to events, and racing quickly captivated the boy.

Stan won the big races, notably the Australian Grand Prix and the New Zealand Grand Prix, and his best machine was a Maserati 250F, one of the most beautiful F1 cars of all time. Jonesey, as his son naturally became known, loved it. He was less enamoured of his father’s generosity to his numerous friends, however, later expressing the regret that some of that expenditure might have been re-directed towards his own racing career.

Instead, he had to do it the hard way. Australia had different minimum ages for driving licences, depending on the state. The lowest available was for 16-year-olds in South Australia, so he established an address there, got his licence at the earliest opportunity, and as soon as he could get a competition version too, he started racing himself.

Karting was popular in Victoria, and soon he was state champion. That led to a Mini 1000 which he and Stan bought for £250 but on which his father lavished nearly four times as much making it into a racing machine. Jonesy spun it on the first corner he drove it through but later used it to win the Victoria Hillclimb Championship.

But it was in 1963 that he took his really first significant steps, with the 2.2-litre Climax-engined Cooper single-seater that Stan also had in his copious garage, and which he eventually let him race in a sprint at Calder; subsequently, Jonesey regularly walloped the locals in their home-built specials.

Then recession hit Stan’s motor business very hard, and Jonesey couldn’t race for several years. Instead he did what many Antipodeans did back then, and headed for England in 1967, with fellow aspiring racer Brian Maguire. They were captivated and vowed to return, and when they did, Jonesey had just £75 in his pocket.

F1 champion Alan Jones passes away, aged 80

His wife Bev lent him £25 to buy a Minivan and he and Brian set about trading them. Eventually they started racing in Formula Ford, but that lacked power and later experiments with an old Lotus 41 led to a shunt and a broken leg. But he used the downtime to focus on the car trading and purchased a damaged Brabham BT28 F3 car from fellow Aussie Alan McCully.

Stan knew Jack Brabham’s partner Ron Tauranac, and after the car had been repaired, Jonesey started racing it in the hotbed of British F3 in late 1970. When he went to the Brazilian F3 Torneio series he started to get noticed, ironically when he started using a ‘bitsa’ engine and traded times with star Aussie Dave Walker, who was driving the works Team Lotus car.

Jonesey, McCully and Maguire then started AIRO (the Australian International Racing Organisation), running BT28s in 1971. They followed up with BT38s in 1972, but the GRD 372 and the Ensign LNF3 were the cars to have that year.

In 1973, Jonesy joined Scotsman Denys Dobbie’s DART team and finally started to break through with their GRD 373. Ironically one of his biggest wins came days after Stan had died, at Silverstone in an older chassis after he’d damaged his regular car. And while he may have been as tough as nails, he admitted that he broke when he received the laurel wreath, which he placed on his father’s coffin on their journey back Down Under for the funeral.

By 1974, when Dobbie’s team had failed, he was lucky to become a regular winner in Formula Atlantic in Harry Stiller’s March. Stiller had once supported Frank Williams and, after recommending Jonesy for a drive that proved hazardous, the two had got together.

Soon he was an established name in British racing, Bev meanwhile running a boarding house for travelling Aussies as they struggled to make ends meet. It was thus a huge surprise when Stiller called to say that he had cancelled tentative plans to go Formula 5000 in 1975 because of the oil crisis, and had instead bought a Hesketh 308B. Suddenly, Jonesey found himself living his dream of driving in F1. In the same car as James Hunt…

He finished seventh with it in the International Trophy race at Silverstone and then made his race debut in the Spanish GP at Montjuich Park, the race in which Rolf Stommelen’s Embassy Hill crashed into the crowd when its rear wing broke. When Stiller suddenly had to close his team, Graham Hill lost no time signing Jonesey as Stommelen’s replacement alongside rising star Tony Brise. At the same time, he also drove John MacDonald’s F5000 March-Cosworth, and suddenly he was on his way, establishing himself as a new hot property.

Such was the reputation he built that he was invited to join former motorcycle and F1 World Champion John Surtees’ F1 team for 1976, and made a big impression when he came close to beating Hunt in the Race of Champions. But Jonesy and Surtees’ relationship became increasingly fractious, and by season-end he was going to quit no matter what the cost to his career.

He fell back into F5000 with Teddy Yip in 1977 – winning the same Australian Grand Prix his father had with the Hong Kong entrepreneur’s Lola T332, and did some USAC Indycar racing, which was less successful. But fate had something else in store.

After Tom Pryce had been killed in the South African GP at Kyalami, Jonesey received a call from team co-owner Jackie Oliver offering him the drive alongside newcomer Ricardo Patrese, who had replaced Pryce’s team-mate Renzo Zorzi. Reckoning that Shadow was one of the few small teams that could be on the verge of success, he accepted. And after a series of strong performances, he finally broke through to win the wet Austrian GP. It would be Shadow’s sole major Grand Grix success and it led to the final stage in his graduation.

The shock win that launched the career of a champion

At the end of the year, Williams restarted his own team after an unhappy time when sponsor Walter Wolf took over the original version. And, crucially, Frank took along designer Patrick Head.

Both were hard-headed men who knew what they wanted, Frank the dreamer who camped out for days before securing Saudi sponsorship, Patrick the non-nonsense pragmatist. He designed a beautiful little car called the FW06, which was sleek but conventional and exactly the sort of machine a new team needed. And now they needed a driver.

In Alan Jones they found the perfect no-nonsense racer. Jonesey was a man whose temperament and general approach to life and racing perfectly meshed with Frank and Patrick’s. Theirs was a match made in F1 heaven.

After a narrow miss in the United States Grand Prix West in 1978, when the front wing broke, the team had a series of strong races: fourth in South Africa; fifth in France; and second in the US GP East. And then for 1979 came Head’s ground effect FW07, the car which harnessed undercar downforce but also allied it to the crucial torsional rigidity that innovator Colin Chapman’s 1978 title-winning Lotus 79 would now be shown to lack as its opposition began to catch up.

Clay Regazzoni scored the revived Williams team’s first win, in the British GP at Silverstone, but Jonesey went on to win the German, Austrian, Dutch and Canadian races and to finish third overall in the World Championship.

The following year he won the Argentine, French, British, Canadian and US GP East races. That string of success cemented the World Championship for Drivers for him as Williams won the World Championship for Constructors after a bitter fight with Nelson Piquet and Brabham, setting Frank and Patrick on their Yellow Brick Road.

Jonesey was always a clean driver, but had that hard, self-reliant edge that all champions need, and Frank and Patrick loved him. He was a man’s man and a tough guy, and you didn’t beat him unless you were pretty special yourself.

That form continued into 1981 when he won the US GP West that opened the season, and the Caesars Palace GP that closed it, but in between was a mixed bag of results and retirements that left him third overall as Piquet narrowly beat Williams’ second driver, Carlos Reutemann. Jonesey never forgave the Argentine when he refused to obey team orders to hand him victory in the Brazilian GP.

A hugely popular racer because of his courage and hard-but-fair, head-down determination, he retired at the end of that 1981 season, but was tempted back very briefly by Arrows in 1983, and then for much longer by the well-sponsored Team Haas (USA) in 1985, after standing in for Mario Andretti at Road America in the team’s CART campaign, where he finished an impressive third. He continued with the team with bespoke Ford power in 1986, but they were still unable to furnish him with winning equipment, and he retired for good from F1 at the end of that season.

He raced Porsches in Australia, became an outspoken F1 commentator for Channel 9, and raced for the next decade or so in the Australian V8 Touring Car series in a variety of cars. His best result was second overall to his own team-mate Glen Seaton in their Ford Falcons in the 1993 series. He ran his own team of Falcons in 1996, but returned to drive for his old boss Tony Longhurst with mixed results before retiring for good in 2002.

Williams outline plans for 50th anniversary year in 2027

He later held the Australian franchise in A1GP, but abandoned plans to compete with other former F1 stars in the Grand Prix Masters race at Kyalami in 2005 when he decided he did not feel physically fit enough for the challenge.

“Alan dedicated his life to motorsport, building a legacy that will live on through the countless people he touched along the way,” his wife Amanda Bulker-Davis said in a statement issued by Motorsport Australia. “Through his achievements, passion and unmistakable character, both on and off the track, Alan left an enduring mark on the sport both nationally and across the globe.

“As a family, we would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who was part of Alan’s journey for the many years of friendship, love and support. He was incredibly fortunate to have so many wonderful people around him.”

title: Liam Lawson makes emotional declaration over Racing Bulls seat uncertainty
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained that the uncertainty around his Racing Bulls F1 future is taking away the "emotion" from his strong grand prix results.

Despite enjoying a standout season, Lawson is still not certain of a place on the 2027 grid, as Racing Bulls evaluate whether to drop him for F2 protege Nikola Tsolov, with Arvid Lindblad expected to be retained for his second season.

Lawson has scored 83 points thus far, 69 of which have been for Racing Bulls, with Lindblad on 38. If Lawson were a constructor by himself, he would be sixth in the standings, only behind his Racing Bulls squad and the top four teams and ahead of Alpine.

However, despite his strong performances, including a run from the pit-lane to ninth on the road in Mexico, before being promoted to seventh after penalties for Oscar Piastri and Franco Colapinto, Lawson has conceded that the uncertainty around his future has taken the emotional edge off his recent strong results.

"It is hard because you want to enjoy the good results as much as possible, and for us, we had a great race; it was a very hard weekend, but we had a great qualifying, and then we had the [disqualification]," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365.

"When we have a race like that, [not knowing about my future] takes away from some of the emotion when it is so undecided about my future.

"With that in the back of your mind, it definitely takes away from some of the results we've had recently."

When then asked if he had a timeline for an announcement, Lawson said that: "It is pretty blurry at the moment, so there is not much indication on when [the decision will be announced]."

[Article continues below]

A tough Mexico weekend

When asked about his demeanour in Mexico after a tough weekend with the Max Verstappen incident in practice before the disqualification from qualifying, Lawson admitted the weekend had been "hard" - but was sure that he would be able to bounce back in Brazil.

"Mexico was just a specific weekend of being hard," Lawson said.

"Today, I feel alright, and coming into this weekend, I feel optimistic about racing here. It is a track I like racing at, so I think Mexico was just a specific thing.

"Every day was just a hard day, with everything that was happening, and even though the race was great, I probably hadn't got over the things that had happened over that weekend.

"I feel like there's not really much else I can do at the moment in this car. We're having a great season, I'm personally having a great season, and we're in a position that we've never been in before.

"But it's nowhere near over, so we're trying to maintain the gap [to Alpine] and at the moment, outside of Mexico, I feel like a lot of the races recently have been really enjoyable and some of the most enjoyable races I've had in a Formula 1 car."

title: Kimi Antonelli unveils beautiful Ayrton Senna tribute after 'emotional' experience
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli will race in an Ayrton Senna tribute helmet at this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, just days after emulating his idol by becoming F1 drivers' champion.

The 20-year-old is now Formula 1's youngest title winner, having beaten Sebastian Vettel's record by over three years at the Mexico City Grand Prix, and celebrated by visiting the Senna family upon reaching Brazil ahead of this weekend.

Like last year, Antonelli visited Senna's resting place. But this time around, he was invited to sit in the cockpit of a #12 Lotus his hero raced.

"I was truly emotional," the Mercedes driver, who also races under that number, told media, including RacingNews365.

"It was a very, very special day that I will remember forever, and that's why I will always be thankful and grateful towards the Senna family for allowing me to see that and to even sit in the car, which was very special. It was an amazing day."

Antonelli revealed the first helmet he will race in F1 with as the champion-elect, which carries the colours from Senna's own helmet, a Brazilian flag and the three-time F1 drivers' champion's famous logo.

Elaborating on his visit to the Senna family, he added: "I actually didn't want to leave. I tried to stay as long as I could there because it was just such a nice experience.

"And the Senna family was very open on showing places where Ayrton used to spend most of his time.

"And it was crazy to think... when I was there, I was like, 'Wow, Ayrton was actually here.' Spending time in his room was very emotional and a very, very special day."

title: Haas announce major new partner as Ferrari star awaits emotional home F1 debut
excerpt:
The arrival of Rafael Camara has already seen a new logo appear on Haas' VF-26.

Haas has announced Banco Bradesco as its first Brazilian commercial partner, with confirmation ahead of the São Paulo Grand Prix weekend.

The timing is no coincidence. Rafael Camara, the Ferrari Driver Academy product signed by Haas on a multi-year deal alongside Oliver Bearman, is set to make his Formula 1 debut at Interlagos, replacing Esteban Ocon who has left the team.

Bradesco, one of Brazil's largest private financial institutions with a market valuation in the region of 45 billion dollars, has backed Camara since his Formula 3 campaign and has now followed him into the top flight.

The bank already carries a significant domestic motorsport footprint, sponsoring Brazilian Stock Car, TCR and Formula 4 Brasil.

The partnership is understood to be substantial, with guesses placing the annual value somewhere between 15 and 25 million US dollars.

That figure would sit comfortably within the range typically commanded by rear wing branding, one of the most visible and lucrative spaces on a Formula 1 car thanks to its constant exposure to rear-facing broadcast cameras.

Bradesco is set to take over that rear wing real estate, replacing Toyota Gazoo Racing in the position.

TGR's technical and commercial partnership with Haas, which began in late 2024 and has been reported to carry a combined value of around 25 million dollars annually, has provided prominent livery integration since its expansion into a title partnership.

[Article continues below]

Reaction from Haas and Banco Bradesco

Reacting, Haas boss Ayao Komatsu spoke of his pride that Banco Bradesco had chosen to enter F1 for the first time with his squad.

"We’re delighted to welcome Bradesco Bank as a partner of Haas F1 Team," he said.

"Bradesco’s entry into Formula 1 for the first time marks an exciting milestone for them as a brand leader, and we’re proud and excited that they’ve chosen to begin that journey with us.

"This is an opportunity to build a partnership that brings the bank closer to fans through the sport and its ever-growing international appeal.

"We look forward to building a strong relationship with Bradesco as we go racing next season and creating dynamic new customer-facing opportunities for them throughout the world."

Speaking on behalf of Banco Bradesco, executive vice president José Ramos Rocha Neto spoke of the similarities between F1 and the banking world.

"Partnering with Haas F1 Team marks an extraordinary milestone in projecting the Bradesco brand onto the highest echelon of global sport," he said.

"Formula 1 embodies innovation, technological precision, high performance, and sophistication, all seamlessly connected with the genuine emotion and passion of fans – attributes that directly reflect our corporate governance and long-term vision at Banco Bradesco.

"Furthermore, this alliance reinforces our enduring commitment to the future of Brazilian motorsport, standing firmly alongside the rising talent of Rafael Câmara and actively empowering the next generation of racing drivers in our country.

"We’re immensely proud to embark on this journey alongside Ayao Komatsu and the entire team, connecting our organisation to millions of passionate motorsport fans in Brazil and worldwide."

title: Max Verstappen hands Kimi Antonelli key advice on being F1 champion

title: Liam Lawson handed double-down verdict in F1 future fight: 'It makes no sense'
excerpt:
Karun Chandhok has doubled down on his assessment that Racing Bulls would be making a mistake by replacing Liam Lawson with Nikola Tsolov for the 2027 season.

The Sky Sports F1 pundit first raised the issue last week and has now reiterated his position, insisting there is no statistical or performance-based justification for such a switch.

Outside the main four teams, Lawson has been F1's standout performer, sitting comfortably in ninth in the drivers' standings, and the mainstay behind his team now on the brink of securing its highest finish in the constructors' championship: fifth.

Whilst Tsolov finished runner-up in F3 last year and is second in the F2 standings with two rounds remaining, Chandhok feels there is no evidence to support dropping New Zealander Lawson in favour of an unproven rookie.

"I don't see how there's any data or information inside, outside, upside down, in between that suggests that Nikola Tsolov is faster, or a better option, than Liam Lawson today, objectively, I just don't understand that," said Chandhok, in the Sky Sports F1 podcast.

"On Friday, I said it would be one of the most unjust sackings in F1 if Liam Lawson lost his seat, and I stand by that.

"Because I think what we have to remember is Toro Rosso, back in the day, was started as a team to bring through young drivers into the top team.

"Sebastian Vettel was the first big export and successful export, and then we had [Max] Verstappen, [Carlos] Sainz etc, but they're in a completely different place.

"I remember being a Red Bull junior back then, and all of us banging on Helmut [Marko]'s door, saying, 'Please, please, please, give me a go'. They're not that team from 20 years ago.

"They've got Max Verstappen as their established number one, who's going to be there for some time longer, so they're not looking to turn over two seats all the time. They're looking to replace one driver now alongside Max."

Chandhok - 'There's no clear benchmark'

Chandhok also warned that axing Lawson would leave Racing Bulls without any experienced reference point for its younger drivers, even if Red Bull has decided Lawson will never return to the senior team.

"Even if you never promote Liam back up [to Red Bull], even if you say, 'Liam had a chance, he blew it. He's not going to go back in the top team. Therefore, that's why we're swapping him', I would still rather have Liam as the reference for any other young juniors coming through," said Chandhok.

"Because if you've got [Arvid] Lindblad in his second season, and Tsolov as the rookie, there's no clear benchmark. There's no clear reference of, 'We don't know how much Lindblad has improved into season two'.

"He could have made a step as big as Kimi Antonelli. He could not. Why have that level of question mark over the performance of the overall team? To me, it just makes no sense.

"I would have Tsolov do a whole bunch of testing and TPC programmes. Clearly, he's a good driver. He's done a great job in F2, but to me, I would just keep the team the same.

"Also now, they're no longer a back-of-the-grid team. They're top of the midfield. That team, there's a lot of commercial money there. There's a lot of prize money there, and to me, I just don't understand why you would change that."

title: Rafael Camara addresses key F2 question ahead of surprise F1 debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara says a decision has not yet been taken on whether he will sacrifice the F2 title after his surprise call-up by Haas.

Haas has drafted its 2027 driver in early for the Sao Paulo GP in place of Ryo Hirakawa, who is racing for the WEC title this weekend, after Esteban Ocon was formally dismissed earlier this week.

In Haas's announcement, no mention was made on who will partner Oliver Bearman in Las Vegas, Qatar, or Abu Dhabi - with Camara on paper, set to go up against Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov in Qatar and Abu Dhabi for the F2 crown.

Camara currently leads the standings by seven points from Tsolov with the two rounds remaining, and given the complexity of running both series on the same weekend, it is likely that if Camara is given the F1 seat for the final three rounds beyond Sao Paulo, he would sacrifice the title.

However, speaking ahead of his grand prix debut, Camara insisted that no decision had been taken, and would not be until after the weekend.

"It is something that we will be discussing after the weekend, on how to prepare for the future," Camara told media, including RacingNews365.

"But I'm not really discussing that at the moment, so I'm just making sure that we do a great time this weekend, and then after that, we will see what happens.

"I don't predict the future, so we will see what will happen. I'm just trying to finish the weekend with everything clean, and then after that, we will see what happens."

[Article continues below]

Bortoleto wades in

Camara's good friend Gabriel Bortoleto won the 2024 F2 title, and had his say on the situation, as he indicated that the rookie should focus on winning the F2 title and having that prestige attached to his name.

"It is a good question, because obviously I was not in the same situation as Rafa, and I think having a title like F2 or F3 to your name, especially when only a few drivers have done it in their first year, is something you are proud to have," Bortoleto said.

"I know racing in F1 is important, but if you already have a contract signed for next season, that is his case- and I had it as well when I was still on the charge for my championship. I think having the F2 title is cool.

"So I'm happy that I stuck to F2 and I did my F2 thing. I won the title, and now I can look back and be like: 'Okay, I'm an F3 champion. I'm an F2 champion, and now I'm in F1, and you have your time to learn.

"Obviously, you want to go to your first season in F1 with the most knowledge possible to not make mistakes or make the least mistakes possible.

"But you know, I think there is no real pressure on [Camara] to need to perform at this race, or you are out. That's not the situation. That was not my situation."

title: Valtteri Bottas reveals 'red zone' Cadillac issue that sparked horrifying crash
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has revealed how his horrifying crash in the Mexico City Grand Prix was caused by his Cadillac running in the "red zone" for too long with brake temperatures.

Approaching Turn 1 at top speed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the left-front suspension completely gave out, exploding in a way similar to Sébastien Buemi's Toro Rosso in China over a decade ago.

It left Bottas a passenger and powerless to prevent a heavy collision with the barriers. After a short while in the stricken MAC-26, the Finnish driver gave the thumbs up to indicate he was okay, before climbing out of the car.

The 10-time grand prix winner explained the extent of his injuries, which were thankfully significantly less severe than they otherwise might have been.

"[There was a bit of] pain, but it is just a muscle bruise, so nothing damaged, and now it feels completely normal," Bottas began to media, including RacingNews365, in his first public comments on the crash.

"These things shouldn't happen, but it happened. The main thing is that we understand why we have certain limits when it comes to temperatures, and we've reviewed those so we could really locate exactly what broke, and why."

Bottas revealed that Cadillac has changed back to some older parts for this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix to alleviate any concerns with the car.

"We've had to revert some parts to the old spec, and we've had to revert the limits on temperatures we can run on those," he explained. "The heat from the brakes has to go somewhere, and at the moment, part of it is going to the wishbones."

Pushed further on the change, Bottas explained that the MAC-26 was running "in the red zone" for too long, with brake issues a problem that has plagued the American team throughout its maiden campaign.

"It is the wishbone mountings, but we've lowered the limits, which shouldn't be an issue here," he said. "We understand that we're just running too long in the red zone. We thought it was safe, but we never tested it by running it so long at that temperature."

[Article continues below]

Bottas on Cadillac suspension in Brazil

Turning to the Interlagos weekend, Bottas was optimistic that the lower temperatures forecast, including rain on Sunday, should mean the issue is not a problem.

"Based on the forecast here, I think we should be okay," he said. "It's going to be quite a bit cooler on Sunday, maybe some rain, so I think here we should be okay, but they are still doing more testing at the factory with the right side of the suspension that is now back in Silverstone.

"They're doing some stress testing and trying to get more accurate temperature limits on both.

"If we didn't understand what broke and why, then you would struggle with confidence, but we understand, and we know now what the limits are, so that's why it's okay.

"Mexico is going to be the hardest one for the rest of the season with the temperatures, so I think we should be okay, but obviously need some good redesigning for the future."

title: Pierre Gasly subject to early-morning drug test ahead of Sao Paulo GP
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly has revealed that he was subject to a random doping test ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend.

F1 drivers are, like other professional athletes, subject to the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) anti-doping rules, with the FIA long complying with WADA's codes.

This involves random drug tests through the year, including during and even before grand prix weekends.

Any missed test is treated as a failure, as happened with Manchester United footballer Rio Ferdinand in 2003, who was then banned from playing for eight months and fined £50,000 GBP.

However, Gasly did not miss his test, as he revealed the test administrators woke him up at 6am on Thursday morning.

Asked if he was optimistic for Interlagos, given he has two podiums at the venue, Gasly indicated he was, as he revealed the drug test.

"You just made my day," he began to tell media, including RacingNews365.

"I got woken up at 06:00 for a doping test this morning, so I'm not in the best mood.

"It was a bad night, but I love this place. It's the only track where I've had two F1 podiums, my first in 2019 and then in 2024 in the rain. And Sunday looks like it is going to rain, so I am very excited."

[Article continues below]

Costly Mexico penalty for Gasly

Gasly also spoke about his costly penalty from Mexico City, where he was banished from the points positions after a severe penalty for not slowing under yellow flags.

The Alpine driver had finished 10th on the road, and was then promoted to ninth after Oscar Piastri's penalty for colliding with Arvid Lindblad to trigger the yellow flags, which caught Gasly, and team-mate Franco Colapinto, out.

Gasly was handed a stop/go penalty for failing to slow, which was converted into a 30-second time penalty, and handed two penalty points on his superlicence, as he fell from ninth to 17th in the final results.

Colapinto was handed a 10-second penalty and one penalty point as he dropped from seventh to 15th - with Alpine's points haul wiped out.

Discussing the incident, Gasly took full responsibility for his failure to adhere to the flags.

"Ultimately, I didn't slow down enough, so I take full responsibility for the penalty," Gasly said.

"For the penalty, I think the circumstances of it were not very easy because the crash happened right in front of us, and I think the double yellow was right as I was at the apex of Turn 1, and I didn't really go back on the throttle, which makes me slow down, but obviously, it wasn't enough for the stewards to be comfortable with it.

"So it was not great, and then after that, I think there was a panel in Turn 3 which showed green, yellow, green, yellow, so the panel didn't quite work, so it was not straightforward, but at the end of the day, it is just annoying that it cost points to the team.

"I've always pushed myself to be strict on yellow flags because it is safety-related, so that's why I'm not going to argue the penalty, because in the situation, it was really safe.

"Lindblad's car was completely to the right; I could see where it was, but nonetheless, if you have a yellow flag in Monaco or Las Vegas, or these types of tracks, we should always slow down, and that's why, to me, I was wrong, and there is no arguing about it.

"But the question of consistency, I think, is quite clear on what needs to be done and what I haven't done.

"Now, we've got a good example of what is not tolerated in a race condition, and I just expect the same for any other driver going forward."

title: Aston Martin air fear-mongering concern over 'uncomfortable' F1 situation
excerpt:
Mike Krack has called out the media for "generating a lot of distraction and a lot of fear unnecessarily" over the uncertain situation in the Middle East as F1 faces the crucial decision whether to race in the region this year.

Formula 1 is scheduled to end the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in late November and early December, but the instability caused by the United States-Iran war means there could still be a last-minute change of plans.

Ahead of this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, Krack was asked how complicated the unresolved situation makes planning for the end of the campaign — with F1's likely contingency plan to head to Imola in place of the two Middle Eastern rounds — and whether staff at Aston Martin are happy to work in the war-torn region.

"So I would say logistics and parts are not really a big deal. You just plan quantities, and then it's about getting them [team personnel] there," the Aston Martin chief trackside engineering officer told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think the staff is a valid question and a good question, because everybody reads the news, everybody reads the internet, and some news is correct, some is less serious

"Unfortunately, these days you get the clicks when you bring the shocking news or the threatening news."

Krack conceded that the team could not give its employees complete guarantees given the fluid and dynamic situation.

"But there are questions raised inside the team because there are families that are asking questions, so it's a difficult subject, and the more reassurance we can give, the better it is. But you cannot always do that," he added.

"You cannot always give 100 per cent reassurance because also often we don't know ourselves what's going to happen."

[Article continues below]

F1 defended over looming decision

Krack voiced his support for F1 and the FIA to make the correct decisions when weighed up against the associated risks, maintaining that the championship and its governing body have "better information" than the team.

"Now I discussed it in length with Andy [Stevenson] this morning, and we are really convinced that F1 is not going to take any unnecessary risks," he said.

"They are aware of the situation. They have much better information than we have, and I think if there is a serious risk, I think they will take the correct action.

"I think at the moment they are still evaluating that situation, and I'm sure they have set themselves some deadlines, which we're not over yet. So I think we need to give them the time to do that. But I would be really surprised if they take risks."

There has been a fresh wave of concern in recent weeks that the United States' mid-term elections may prompt Donald Trump to instigate new attacks on Iran, which in turn could provoke retaliation.

However, the results of those elections have likely reduced the chance of any impending military action, with the Democrats reclaiming control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

With the United States-Iran War and the associated effects a significant factor in heavy Republican defeats across the nation, Trump is perhaps less willing to further inflame the situation.

Nonetheless, the Iranian state has released a list of "zero-hour targets" that it would seek to strike in such an eventuality, many of which are hotels used by F1 and other forms of motorsport when visiting Qatar.

MotoGP races at the Lusail International Circuit this weekend, and Formula 1 will no doubt be watching with bated breath.

Krack argued that much of the coverage on the matter is "not helping" the broader situation or how those working in Formula 1 feel about visiting the region, which has already seen the Bahrain Grand Prix relocated to Malaysia and the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix cancelled altogether.

"People read these things and the first thing you do, you check, is my hotel in that list? But it doesn't really matter, does it, because you can change at any time," he said.

"But this is the kind of news that is not helping at the moment, and it is generating a lot of distraction and a lot of fear unnecessarily. But as I said, I think F1 is aware of it; everyone is also reading these things, so I think they take the right steps.

"It's always these situations where you know you are a bit left in the unknown, which makes people very uncomfortable. And it's the same for everyone. It's the same for me as well; you don't know what's going to happen."

title: Are stricter Ferrari rules needed after latest Lewis Hamilton-Charles Leclerc clash?
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will face the media in São Paulo, with the pair's Mexico City clash an expected talking point.

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton collided on the opening lap in Mexico City, running wide together at Turn 4 as Leclerc attempted an outside move on his teammate for the lead.

Both cars ran off the circuit, with Leclerc cutting across the grass at Turn 5 to retake first place while Hamilton rejoined the track and lost second to Max Verstappen.

Stewards handed Leclerc a five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining a lasting advantage, reduced from ten seconds because Hamilton had also run wide.

Telemetry later showed Leclerc carried a 15 km/h slipstream advantage into the corner and braked 25 metres later than Hamilton, making it near-impossible for both cars to stay within track limits.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur rejected suggestions that the circuit layout was to blame, instead pointing to overly combative racing between the two drivers and a lack of respect for the team's wider interests.

Three Ferrari intra-team incidents but still Fred Vasseur resists change

This was far from the first sign of friction between the Ferrari duo this season. At the Dutch Grand Prix, tensions surfaced when Hamilton was held up behind Leclerc on a differing strategy, with Leclerc accused of delaying a pit call rather than yielding.

At Monza, the pair had an on-track confrontation at the first corner on the opening lap that prompted Hamilton to call for clearer driver protocols within the team.

Despite the repeated incidents, Vasseur has continued to resist introducing written rules of engagement, preferring to rely on shared principles and post-race debriefs rather than prescriptive team orders.

With Mexico marking the third significant flashpoint of the campaign, RacingNews365 wants to know what you think: does Ferrari need to get stricter with Hamilton and Leclerc before another collision costs the team more than just five seconds?

title: Toto Wolff delivers clear F1 title message ahead of 'demanding weekend'
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has made clear that Mercedes' championship ambitions do not end with Kimi Antonelli's drivers' title, insisting there is still "a job left to finish" as the team turns its attention to the constructors' battle at Interlagos this weekend.

Antonelli sealed his maiden world championship in Mexico City on Sunday, finishing third behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton to confirm the title with four races to spare, becoming the youngest world champion in F1 history.

Heading into the São Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday, Mercedes holds a 126-point lead over Ferrari in the constructors' standings.

The Brackley-based squad will clinch the teams' title if it outscores Ferrari by at least three points across the weekend, while Ferrari needs a four-point swing in its favour to keep the fight alive heading to Las Vegas.

Ferrari has outscored Mercedes over the last four race weekends, despite the opening-lap clash between Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in Mexico City.

Initially reflecting on the significance of Antonelli's triumph and Russell's season, team principal Wolff said: "Mexico was a special weekend for Kimi and the team.

"Winning the world championship is an incredible achievement, particularly at this stage of his career, and he thoroughly deserves the moment.

"For George, there is natural disappointment. He has been hard on himself, but he has driven at an incredibly high level this season and shown again the quality we know he has.

"There have been circumstances out of his control that haven't always fallen his way, and we have not always given him the car to perform.

"Nevertheless, the way he has continued to push and contribute to the team says so much about him."

[Article continues below]

Wolff - 'Nothing is won yet'

Wolff then shifted the spotlight to the task still at hand in Brazil.

"Our focus, though, has already moved to São Paulo," he added. "We came into this season wanting to fight for both championships, and there is still a job left to finish.

"The teams' title is about the performance of the entire operation, both at the track and back in Brackley and Brixworth, and securing it would mean a great deal to all of us.

"Nothing is won yet, though. Interlagos is always a demanding weekend, and there is little margin for error.

"We need to execute strongly from the first session and put ourselves in the best possible position to bring home both titles this season."

title: Kimi Antonelli pays Ayrton Senna family emotional visit: 'An unforgettable day'
excerpt:
After becoming world champion in Mexico City, Kimi Antonelli went somewhere incredibly special.

Kimi Antonelli paid a visit to Ayrton Senna's nephew and nieces ahead of this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, describing it as an "unforgettable day"

Senna has long been the guiding inspiration behind Antonelli's career. The Italian grew up on stories of the three-time champion and has idolised him since childhood, a tribute reflected in his choice of race number.

Antonelli carries number 12, the number Senna used for part of his own career, and will keep it again next season purely to honour him.

For Antonelli, Senna is far more than a former Formula 1 driver, he is a source of inspiration. That made his visit to the Senna family all the more significant.

Upon arriving in Brazil after becoming world champion in Mexico City, Antonelli travelled with his father Marco to spend time with Bruno, Bianca and Paula Senna, Ayrton's nephew and nieces.

The new world champion shared a photo on Instagram of himself sitting in the legendary Lotus 98T, the car in which Senna won the Spanish and Detroit Grands Prix in 1986. It carried the same number 12.
